'''Mary Lowe Good''' (June 20, 1931 – November 20, 2019) was an American inorganic chemist who worked academically, in industrial research and in government. Good contributed to the understanding of [[catalysts]] such as [[ruthenium]].<ref name=Yount>{{cite book|last1=Yount|first1=Lisa|title=A to Z of women in science and math|date=2008|publisher=Facts On File|location=New York|isbn=978-0816066957|pages=108–109 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=428i2UdWRRAC&pg=PA108|access-date=7 April 2015}}{{unreliable source?|date=May 2018}}</ref><ref name=UALRNews2012/>

Good served as the Under Secretary for Technology in the [[United States Department of Commerce]] from 1993 to 1997 under President [[Bill Clinton]]. She briefly served as Acting [[United States Secretary of Commerce]] from April 3, 1996, to April 12, 1996.<ref name="Notebook">{{cite news |title=Notebook |url=https://www.the-scientist.com/notebook-old/notebook-57427 |website=The Scientist|date=June 23, 1997|issue=June |access-date=17 December 2019}}</ref><ref name="Fields">{{cite web |last1=Fields |first1=Craig |title=MARY L. GOOD Under Secretary for Technology, United States Department of Commerce |url=https://clintonwhitehouse3.archives.gov/WH/EOP/OSTP/forum/html/good.html |website=White House Forum on the Role of Science and Technology |access-date=17 December 2019|date=March 29–30, 1995}}</ref>

Good received a number of significant awards including the [[Garvan–Olin Medal]], the [[Othmer Gold Medal]], the [[Priestley Medal]], the [[Vannevar Bush Award]], and the [[Heinz Awards|Heinz Award]] in Technology, the Economy, and Employment.<ref name=LittleRock>{{cite web|title=Dr. Mary Good Founding Dean|url=http://ualr.edu/eit/mary-good/|website=George W. Donaghey College of Engineering and Information Technology|publisher=University of Kansas at Little Rock|access-date=2013-06-22|archive-date=2018-11-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181116085853/https://ualr.edu/eit/mary-good/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
{{external media | width = 210px | float = right | headerimage=[[File:Mary Lowe Good Women in Chemistry from video.png|210px]]  | video1 = Mary Lowe Good, [https://www.sciencehistory.org/historical-profile/mary-lowe-good "You've got to take the opportunities as they appear"],  [[Science History Institute]] |video2 = [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PcXtXyNtWNE Dr. Mary Good Interview], Arkansas Academy of Computing History }}

Mary Lowe was born on June 20, 1931, in [[Grapevine, Texas]], to Winnie and John Lowe.<ref name=GoodOralHistory>{{cite web|author=Center for Oral History| title=Mary L. Good |url=https://oh.sciencehistory.org/oral-histories/good-mary-l|website=[[Science History Institute]] }}</ref><ref name="Moreau"/> The family moved to [[Kirby, Arkansas]], in 1942. Her father was a principal in a local school,<ref name=GoodOralHistory/> and her mother was a teacher and librarian.<ref name=Yount/> The family later moved to [[Willisville, Arkansas]], where Mary attended high school.<ref name=GoodOralHistory/> No chemistry course or lab was offered at the school, so Mary would spend her time as a young student creating her own labs. She once produced a homemade photography studio in the cellar of her home after fixing up an old enlarger and reading up on the chemicals needed for photo developing.<ref name=GoodOralHistory/>

Lowe initially attended Arkansas State Teacher's College (now the [[University of Central Arkansas]]) with the intention of being a home economics teacher. She became interested in chemistry as a freshman and changed her major to chemistry and physics, receiving her B.Sc. from the [[University of Central Arkansas]] in 1950. Lowe became one of the first three students to graduate from the University's chemistry program.<ref name=GoodDistinction>{{cite web|author=Arkansas PBS| title=Mary L. Good |url=http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Vc7TIkrRzgc  |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211214/Vc7TIkrRzgc |archive-date=2021-12-14 |url-status=live|website=[[Arkansas PBS]] | date=9 January 2015 }}{{cbignore}}</ref>

Her professors encouraged her to go to graduate school. She received a fellowship, which enabled her to study [[radiochemistry]] with Raymond R. Edwards at the [[University of Arkansas]]. At age 19, as an atomic energy research assistant, she received her first [[Q clearance|Q-level government clearance]].<ref name=GoodOralHistory/> In 1952, she married Bill Jewel Good, a fellow graduate student in physics.<ref name=Yount/><!-- Good, Bill J. later Professor Emeritus of Physics and Dean Emeritus of the College of Sciences; Ph.D., Louisiana State University --> Mary Lowe Good received her MS in 1953 and her PhD in 1955 from the [[University of Arkansas]] becoming the first woman from Arkansas to earn a doctoral degree in the hard sciences.<ref name=GoodOralHistory/><ref name=CHF>{{cite web|title=Mary Lowe Good|url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/historical-profile/mary-lowe-good|publisher=[[Science History Institute]]|access-date=22 June 2013}}</ref><ref name="Transcript">{{cite book|first= James G. |last=Traynham|title=Mary L. Good, Transcript of an Interview Conducted by James G. Traynham at Little Rock, Arkansas on 2 June 1998 |date=2 June 1998 |url=https://oh.sciencehistory.org/sites/default/files/good_ml_0171_suppl.pdf|place=Philadelphia, PA|publisher=[[Chemical Heritage Foundation]] }}</ref><ref name=GoodEncyclopedia>{{cite web|author=Encyclopedia of Arkansas| title=Mary Lowe Good (1931–2019) |url=https://encyclopediaofarkansas.net/entries/mary-lowe-good-8860/ |website=[[Encyclopedia of Arkansas]] }}</ref> Her graduate work involved studying [[Iodine-131|radioactive iodine]] in [[aqueous solution]]s (used for treating [[hyperthyroidism|thyroid conditions]]). She worked on processes of [[solvent extraction]] of [[metal complexes]] and described the chemical and physical properties of [[chemical species]] in an [[organic solvent]].<ref name=Wayne/> She was able to explain why solutions of [[radioactive iodine]] were unstable, and determine the concentration at which species would be at equilibrium values, by applying the [[Nernst equation]] effect.<ref name=GoodOralHistory/>

==Louisiana State University System==
Good spent 25 years in teaching and research at [[Louisiana State University]] and the [[University of New Orleans]], which was at the time part of the [[Louisiana State University System]].<ref name=LittleRock/> Good went to Baton Rouge as director of the radiochemistry laboratory and as an instructor and assistant professor of chemistry (1954–1958). At Baton Rouge she worked on [[iodine]] and [[sulfur]] chemistry with Sean McGlynn.<ref name=GoodOralHistory/><ref name="Moreau"/>

In 1958 Good and her husband moved to New Orleans when both were offered positions at a new campus that was being established.<ref name=GoodOralHistory/> The Louisiana State University New Orleans (LSUNO) was the first university in the southern states to open as a fully integrated institution.<ref name=LSUNO>{{cite news|title=University of New Orleans Honors First African-American Students|url=http://www.uno.edu/news/2013/UniversityofNewOrleansHonorsFirstAfricanAmericanStudents.aspx|access-date=8 April 2015|work=UNO News|date=March 13, 2013}}</ref> Expanding on her work in radiochemistry, Good became interested in using [[spectroscopy]] to study inorganic chemistry compounds, taking measurements and relating experimental results to theoretical predictions. She was able to study molecular bonding in both solutions and solid states.<ref name=GoodOralHistory/><ref name=Wayne/> She also was able to extract [[rhodium]] complexes, using organic solvents, and demonstrate that they were bimetallic.<ref name=GoodOralHistory/>

Good moved up the academic ranks to become the Boyd Professor of Chemistry at New Orleans (1974–1978),<ref name=GoodOralHistory/> the first woman to achieve the university's most distinguished rank.<ref name=ACM2013>{{cite book|title=American Chemical Society Division of the History of Chemistry Program and Abstracts April 7–11, 2013|date=April 11, 2013|publisher=American Chemical Society|url=http://www.scs.illinois.edu/~mainzv/HIST/meetings/2013-spring/HIST%20Spring%202013%20Program%20Abstracts%20Only.pdf |access-date=7 April 2015}}</ref> From 1978 to 1980, she returned to [[Baton Rouge]] to develop a new program as the Boyd Professor of Materials Science, Division of Engineering Research.<ref name=GoodOralHistory/>

Good was one of the first people to use [[Mössbauer spectroscopy]] techniques for basic chemical research.<ref name=Wayne>{{cite book|last1=Wayne|first1=Tiffany K.|title=American women of science since 1900|date=2011|publisher=ABC-CLIO|location=Santa Barbara, Calif.|isbn=978-1598841589|pages=445–446|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gPGZJ_YuMwgC&pg=PA445|access-date=7 April 2015}}</ref> Mössbauer spectroscopy enables researchers to study the interactions of [[gamma rays]] with matter, observing very small differences in the energy of electrons within atoms. This data can be used to identify the molecular structure of complicated compounds containing metal ions.<ref name=Yount/>

Good contributed to the understanding of [[catalysts]] such as [[ruthenium]]. At that time, no one had attempted to observe Mössbauer effects in ruthenium, in part because it had to be examined at extremely low temperatures, cooled by [[liquid helium]]. Good was able to study ruthenium, which exists in a variety of [[oxidation states]], and derive detailed chemical and structural information.<ref name=Wayne/>

She also did work in materials science on the physical and biological investigations of marine antifouling coatings, used to remove barnacles from ships.<ref name="Wayne"/>  Her publications include more than 100 articles in refereed journals<ref name=STEMBlog/> and several books.<ref name=Wayne/>

==American Chemical Society==
Good was the first woman to be elected to the board of the [[American Chemical Society]] in 1972.<ref name="Moreau"/> She was elected ACS Board Chairman in 1978 and 1980,<ref name=ACSBoardChair>{{cite journal|title=Mary Good elected ACS Board Chairman|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|date=December 12, 1977|volume=55|issue=50|page=7|doi=10.1021/cen-v055n050.p007}}</ref> and became ACS President elect as of 1986, serving as president in 1987.<ref name=President>{{cite journal|title=Mary Good wins ACS presidential election|journal= Chemical & Engineering News|date=November 18, 1985|volume=63|issue=46|pages=5–6|doi=10.1021/cen-v063n046.p005}}</ref><ref name=C&EN1996>{{cite magazine|title=Mary Lowe Good To Receive 1997 Priestley Medal |url=http://pubs.acs.org/cen/hotarticles/cenear/960513/medal.html |access-date=2 February 2015|magazine=Chemical & Engineering News|publisher=American Chemical Society|date=May 13, 1996}}</ref>

==International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry==
Good was also elected President of the [[IUPAC Inorganic Chemistry Division|inorganic chemistry division]]  of the [[International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry]] (IUPAC) in 1981, and held the position until 1985, for two terms. She was the first woman to be elected a division head of IUPAC.<ref name="Moreau"/><ref name="IUPAC">{{cite journal |title=Mary Good elected IUPAC division president |journal=Chemical & Engineering News |date=7 September 1981 |volume=59 |issue=36 |page=9 |doi=10.1021/cen-v059n036.p009}}</ref>

As head of  the  inorganic chemistry  division, she was responsible for overseeing the  work  of  the commissions  on nomenclature  for inorganic  chemistry; the [[Commission on Isotopic Abundances and Atomic Weights]], and the commission on high  temperatures   and   refractory   materials.  Her work included supervising a complete revision of the [[IUPAC nomenclature of inorganic chemistry]] or "Red Book".<ref name="IUPAC"/>

In addition to holding the position of division president (1980–1985), Good served on  IUPAC's  Governing  Bureau (1985–1993).<ref name="Long"/> 
She became an elected member (EM) of the bureau after her second term as division president, and served on the Executive Committee (EC) of IUPAC from 1985 to 1993.<ref name="Moreau"/>
In 1989, Good was instrumental in introducing the "Chemistry in Action" program, encouraging IUPAC members to become active and visible leaders in areas of scientific and social importance, including the atmosphere and  the environment, energy  processes, advanced materials, and bio-technology.<ref name="O'Sullivan">{{cite journal |last1=O'Sullivan |first1=Dermot A. |title=New IUPAC program broadens organization's scope |journal=Chemical & Engineering News |date=18 September 1989 |volume=67 |issue=38 |pages=25–27 |doi=10.1021/cen-v067n038.p025}}</ref><ref name="Moreau">{{cite journal |last1=Moreau |first1=Nicole |title=Women's Increasing Responsibilities in IUPAC since 1975 |journal=Chemistry International |date=1 July 2019 |volume=41 |issue=3 |pages=53–55 |doi=10.1515/ci-2019-0317|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Good also served on the board of directors of the  [[Industrial Research Institute]] (IRI, 1982-1987).<ref name="Long"/>

==Industrial career==
In 1980, Mary Lowe Good was approached to become head of the Engineered Materials Research division at Signal Research Center, Inc.<ref name="Yount"/> (previously Universal Oil Products, later [[AlliedSignal|Allied-Signal Inc.]]), with a staff of 400 scientists and technicians and annual sales of approximately $3 billion.<ref name=Chicago10>{{cite news|title=Chicago's 10 Most Powerful Women |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/1987/11/18/chicagos-10-most-powerful-women/|access-date=7 April 2015|work=Chicago Tribune|date=November 18, 1987}}</ref> In 1981 Mary Good was chosen as vice-president and director of research. She headed the Research Center during a period of significant changes (ownership, mergers, acquisitions and divestitures), maintaining a focus on new technology development and its licensing and commercialization. She became president and director of research for Signal Research Center in 1985, and president of Allied-Signal Engineered Materials Research in 1986<ref name=Yount/> and then the senior vice-president of technology, coordinating the activities of three research centers.<ref name=ACM2013/><ref name=Happy>{{cite journal|title=Alumna focus: Dr. Mary Good Class of 1950|journal=University of Central Arkansas|date=December 2011|pages=50–51|url=http://uca.edu/cnsm/files/2011/12/December-Newsletter-2011.pdf|access-date=7 April 2015|archive-date=17 January 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150117085105/http://uca.edu/cnsm/files/2011/12/December-Newsletter-2011.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Government service==
Mary Lowe Good held government positions under the administrations of four presidents: [[Jimmy Carter]], [[Ronald Reagan]], [[George H. W. Bush]], and [[Bill Clinton]].<ref name="Moreau"/>

In 1980 she was appointed to the National Science Board of the [[National Science Foundation]] by Jimmy Carter. In 1986 she was appointed to it again by Ronald Reagan.<ref name=Heinz>{{cite web|title=The Heinz Awards: Mary Good |url=http://www.heinzawards.net/recipients/mary-good|publisher=The Heinz Awards}}</ref> From 1988 to 1991, she was the first woman to chair  the board.<ref name="Yount"/>  In 1991 President Bush appointed her to the [[President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology]] (PCAST).<ref name=Wessner>{{cite book|editor-last1=Wessner|editor-first1=Charles W.|title=Understanding research, science, and technology parks: global best practices : report of a symposium|date=2009|publisher=National Academies Press|location=Washington, DC|isbn=978-0-309-13789-8|page=148|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5fRjAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA148|access-date=8 April 2015}}</ref> All three positions were part-time commitments, held during the period in which she worked at Allied-Signal Inc.

In 1993, Good left Allied Signal to take a four-year full-time position as the Under Secretary of Commerce for Technology in the [[Technology Administration]], under the Clinton Administration.<ref name=CHF/>  During this time Good led the Clean Car Initiative to develop a hybrid gas-electric car.<ref name="Yount"/>  She encouraged the government to fund basic research and emerging technologies.<ref name="Yount"/> Good was appointed Acting [[United States Secretary of Commerce]] on April 3, 1996, following the death of [[Ronald H. Brown]], until [[Mickey Kantor]] was appointed 9 days later by [[Bill Clinton]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Clinton Appoints Interim Leader for Commerce Dept.|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1996-04-06-fi-55470-story.html |access-date=20 February 2018|work=Los Angeles Times|date=April 6, 1996}}</ref>

==University of Arkansas at Little Rock==
In 1997 Good became the Donaghey University Professor at the [[University of Arkansas at Little Rock]].  She also became the founding dean of the George W. Donaghey College of Engineering and Information Technology (EIT).<ref name="ualr">{{cite web|title=Dr. Mary Good Founding Dean, George W. Donaghey College of Engineering and Information Technology (EIT).|url=http://ualr.edu/eit/mary-good/|publisher=University of Little Rock Arkansas|access-date=22 June 2013|archive-date=16 November 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181116085853/https://ualr.edu/eit/mary-good/|url-status=dead}}</ref> She retired July 1, 2011, becoming dean emeritus of the College of Engineering and Information Technology at the University of Arkansas-Little Rock and special advisor to the chancellor for economic development.<ref name=STEMBlog>{{cite web|title=STEM Woman Leader of the Day- Dr. Mary Good (ASTRA) |url=http://blog.stemconnector.org/stem-woman-leader-day-dr-mary-good-astra|website=STEMBlog|access-date=7 April 2015}}</ref>

==Other activities==
In 1976 Mary Lowe Good was initiated into the Beta Phi chapter of [[Alpha Chi Sigma]] at the South Dakota School of Mines.<ref name=AlphaChi>{{cite web|title=Alpha Chi Sigma Hall of Fame|url=http://www.alphachisigma.org/page.aspx?pid=268|publisher=Alpha Chi Sigma Fraternity|access-date=22 June 2013}}</ref>

She was member for Fund for Arkansas, LLC and Stage 1 Diagnostics, and served on the boards of Delta Trust & Bank and St. Vincent Infirmary, [[Biogen Idec]], [[IDEXX Laboratories]], [[Cincinnati Milling Machine Company|Cincinnati Milacron]], [[Ameritech]],  [[LiveRamp|Acxiom Corporation]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Mary L. Good Profile |url=https://people.forbes.com/profile/mary-l-good/1213 |work=[[Forbes]] |access-date=26 October 2011}}{{dead link|date=January 2022|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref>

From 1988 to 1993 Mary L. Good was president of [[Zonta International|Zonta International Foundation]], an organization supporting the involvement of women in business and science, and the improvement internationally of their legal, political, economic, educational and health status.<ref name="Yount"/><ref name="Wayne"/><ref name=Zonta>{{cite web|title=Past International Foundation Presidents|url=https://www.zonta.org/Portals/0/PDFs/New%20PDFs/Past%20International%20Foundation%20Presidents%20List%20July%201%202014.pdf|website=Zonta International Foundation|access-date=8 April 2015}}</ref>

Good was the founding Chairman of ASTRA, the Alliance for Science & Technology Research in America, beginning in 2000. She was a strong proponent of STEM education and a supporter of women in technology, and was recognized as a national leader in this area.<ref name=UALRNews2012>{{cite news|title=Mary Good Named to National STEM Hall|url=http://ualr.edu/news/2012/06/13/mary-good-named-to-national-stem-hall/|access-date=8 April 2015|work=University of Arkansas at Little Rock News|date=June 13, 2012}}</ref>

The American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS) elected Good to serve as the president in 2001.<ref name=AAAS>{{cite web|title=AAAS Presidents|url=http://archives.aaas.org/people/plist.php?type=President|website=AAAS Archives & Records Center|access-date=7 April 2015}}</ref>

==Death==
Good died at her home in [[Little Rock, Arkansas|Little Rock]], [[Arkansas]], on November 20, 2019, at the age of 88.<ref>[https://www.arkansasbusiness.com/article/129067/mary-good-pioneering-arkansas-scientist-dies-at-88 Mary Good, Pioneering Arkansas Scientist, Dies at 88]</ref>
